questions.stem: Clark Kent, 40, is in ED. His first words are that this is the worst headache of his life. He is a bit muddled and answers short, simple questions best. Which single history question best tells you whether this is a thunderclap headache that needs urgent investigation for subarachnoid haemorrhage?
options: Where exactly in your head is the pain right now?
Did you see flashing lights or zigzags before the pain began?
How quickly did the pain reach its worst after it started?
Is the headache worse when you cough, sneeze or strain?
questions.why: A thunderclap headache is defined by its onset: it reaches maximum intensity within seconds to a minute. Treat it as SAH until proven otherwise, whatever its site or character.
notes: SAH headache can be anywhere, often generalised or occipital, so the site does not separate thunderclap headache from other severe headaches.
This asks about migraine aura. Having no aura does not rule out SAH, and aura does not tell you how fast the headache came on.
Headache that is worse with coughing or straining is a feature of raised ICP or a mass lesion. It does not define a sudden-onset thunderclap headache.

questions.stem: Clark Kent, 40, has an aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage from a 7 mm ACom aneurysm with early hydrocephalus. Neurosurgery is coming to place an EVD and plan securing of the aneurysm. His coagulation is normal and his eGFR is 70. Which medication order should you chart to reduce the risk of a poor outcome from delayed cerebral ischaemia?
options: Nimodipine 60 mg orally or via NG tube every 4 hours for 21 days
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV every 8 hours until the aneurysm is secured
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV every 12 hours for 7 days
Glyceryl trinitrate infusion titrated to a systolic BP below 120 mmHg
questions.why: Oral or NG nimodipine 60 mg 4-hourly for 21 days improves outcome after aneurysmal SAH by reducing delayed cerebral ischaemia. If it causes hypotension, split the dose to 30 mg 2-hourly rather than stopping it.
notes: Antifibrinolytics reduce rebleeding but do not improve functional outcome and may increase ischaemic complications, so they are not routine.
Corticosteroids have no proven benefit in aneurysmal SAH and cause hyperglycaemia. Raised ICP here is from hydrocephalus, not vasogenic oedema.
GTN dilates cerebral vessels and can raise ICP. Pushing SBP below 120 lowers cerebral perfusion pressure; neurosurgery or ICU should set the BP target.

questions.stem: At 15:25 Clark's GCS falls from 13 to 11. His BP rises to 204/100, his HR falls to 48 and his breathing becomes irregular. CT showed early hydrocephalus. His potassium is 4.2 and his only regular medicine is amlodipine. What best explains the fall in his heart rate?
options: Hypokalaemia from repeated vomiting slowing sinoatrial node firing
Amlodipine building up with reduced kidney function and slowing AV conduction
Catecholamine-induced myocardial stunning causing complete heart block
Baroreceptors sensing the surge in BP and triggering reflex vagal slowing
questions.why: Rising ICP lowers cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP = MAP − ICP). Brainstem ischaemia drives a sympathetic surge that raises MAP to protect perfusion, and carotid and aortic baroreceptors respond with vagal bradycardia (the Cushing response). This is why you do not chase the BP down.
notes: His potassium is normal at 4.2. Hypokalaemia tends to cause tachyarrhythmias and ectopy, not sinus bradycardia.
Amlodipine is a dihydropyridine that is cleared by the liver and does not slow the SA or AV node; it more often causes reflex tachycardia.
Neurogenic stunned myocardium in SAH causes ECG changes and LV dysfunction with hypotension, not this pattern of hypertension, bradycardia and falling GCS.

questions.stem: The nurse looking after Clark, 40, who has SAH, hydrocephalus and a falling GCS, is told to report a new unilateral dilated, unreactive pupil as a sign of transtentorial (uncal) herniation. Why does this herniation dilate the pupil?
options: The expanding aneurysm presses directly on the optic chiasm
The abducens nerve is stretched over the petrous temporal apex
Sympathetic fibres on the internal carotid artery are compressed
The oculomotor nerve is compressed against the tentorial edge
questions.why: In uncal herniation the medial temporal lobe pushes the oculomotor nerve (CN III) against the free edge of the tentorium. Its parasympathetic pupillomotor fibres run on the outside of the nerve, so they are hit first and the pupil on that side becomes fixed and dilated.
notes: Pressure on the chiasm causes a bitemporal field defect, not a fixed dilated pupil. The pupil light reflex is mostly spared.
Abducens stretch from raised ICP causes a lateral rectus palsy (false localising sign), not pupil dilation.
Damage to the sympathetic fibres causes Horner's syndrome with a small (miotic) pupil, not a dilated one.
